q: Who wrote the 1850 novel The Scarlet Letter?
x: Set in Puritan Boston, it follows Hester Prynne, who must wear a scarlet 'A'. Hawthorne added a preface about finding the old manuscript in a customs house.

q: Who wrote the anti-slavery novel Uncle Tom's Cabin?
x: Published in 1852, it sold hundreds of thousands of copies within a few years and stirred anti-slavery feeling in the North.

q: What is the name of Don Quixote's loyal squire?
x: Sancho is a simple farmer who joins Don Quixote hoping to be rewarded with the governorship of an island.

q: Who wrote The Adventures of Pinocchio?
x: Collodi serialized the tale in an Italian children's magazine from 1881. It has been translated into over 200 languages.

q: Which Welsh poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
x: Thomas wrote the poem for his dying father in 1951. He is also known for the radio play Under Milk Wood.

q: Who wrote the Russian novel The Master and Margarita?
x: Bulgakov wrote it in secret in the 1930s. It was not published until the 1960s, long after his death, and features a devil visiting Moscow.

q: Which Colombian author wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude?
x: Published in 1967, the novel tells of the Buendia family in the town of Macondo. Garcia Marquez won the Nobel Prize in 1982.

q: Which Nigerian author wrote Things Fall Apart?
x: Published in 1958, it is among the most widely read African novels. Its title comes from a poem by W. B. Yeats.

q: In Victor Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris, what is the hunchbacked bell-ringer called?
x: Hugo's 1831 novel helped revive interest in the neglected Notre-Dame cathedral and spurred its restoration.

q: Which Shakespeare play features the magician Prospero?
x: Prospero is the exiled Duke of Milan who lives on an island with his daughter Miranda. The play is thought to be among Shakespeare's last.

q: Who is the scheming villain who manipulates Othello?
x: Iago plants the false idea that Othello's wife Desdemona is unfaithful. He is one of Shakespeare's most notorious villains.

q: In King Lear, which daughter refuses to flatter her father with grand speeches?
x: Cordelia says she loves Lear as a daughter should. He banishes her, a decision that leads to disaster.

q: In which year did William Shakespeare die?
x: Tradition says he died on April 23, 1616, which was also his birthday. Cervantes died the same year.

q: The subtitle of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein refers to which figure from Greek myth?
x: The full title is Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humans.

q: What term describes a novel told through letters?
x: Samuel Richardson's Pamela and Clarissa are classic examples. Dracula and Frankenstein also use letters and journals in their telling.

q: What is a word that imitates the sound it describes, such as 'buzz' or 'sizzle', called?
x: The term comes from Greek words meaning 'name-making'. Comics use onomatopoeia heavily for sound effects.

q: How many syllables are in a standard line of iambic pentameter?
x: Each line has five iambs, with an unstressed then stressed syllable. Shakespeare used it for much of his verse.

q: Which Romantic poet wrote 'Ode on a Grecian Urn'?
x: Keats wrote it in 1819. It ends with the line 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty.' He died of tuberculosis aged 25.

q: In Coleridge's The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, what type of bird does the mariner shoot?
x: The dead bird is hung around his neck as punishment. This is the origin of the phrase 'an albatross around one's neck.'

q: Which poet wrote 'The Tyger', which begins 'Tyger Tyger, burning bright'?
x: Blake published it in his 1794 collection Songs of Experience. He also engraved and painted his own books.

q: Which American poet wrote 'The Road Not Taken'?
x: Frost published it in 1916. It begins 'Two roads diverged in a yellow wood' and is often misread as a poem about bold individualism.

q: In which US state did Emily Dickinson spend almost her entire life?
x: She lived in Amherst, Massachusetts. Only a handful of her nearly 1,800 poems were published while she was alive.

q: Which poet published the collection Leaves of Grass in 1855?
x: Whitman revised and expanded the book throughout his life. He paid for the first edition himself.

q: Which Edgar Allan Poe story from 1841 is often called the first modern detective story?
a: The Murders in the Rue Morgue
The Fall of the House of Usher
x: It introduced the brilliant amateur detective C. Auguste Dupin, a model for Sherlock Holmes.

q: Where is the novel Wuthering Heights set?
x: The Bronte sisters grew up at Haworth in Yorkshire, on the edge of the wild moors that shaped the novel's atmosphere.

q: What name did Thomas Hardy give to the region of southwest England in his novels?
x: Hardy's Wessex is based on Dorset and neighboring counties. The name revived the old Anglo-Saxon kingdom.

q: Under which pen name did Charlotte Bronte publish Jane Eyre?
x: The three Bronte sisters all used male-sounding pseudonyms with the initials C, E and A.

q: What was the real name of the novelist who wrote as George Eliot?
x: Evans chose a male pen name so her fiction would be taken seriously. Her works include Middlemarch and Silas Marner.

q: What was Mark Twain's real name?
x: The name 'Mark Twain' comes from a riverboat call meaning two fathoms deep. Clemens was once a Mississippi riverboat pilot.

q: What was George Orwell's real name?
x: Blair took the pen name Orwell after the River Orwell in Suffolk. He was born in India in 1903.

q: Who is the orphan hero of Dickens's novel Great Expectations?
x: Pip rises from a village blacksmith's apprentice to a gentleman in London. The novel was serialized in 1860-61.

q: What does Don Quixote famously attack, believing them to be giants?
x: The scene gave English the phrase 'tilting at windmills', meaning to fight imaginary enemies.

q: In The Lord of the Rings, in which land does Mount Doom lie?
x: Mordor is the realm of the Dark Lord Sauron. The Ring can only be destroyed in the fires where it was forged.

q: Who wrote the science fiction epic Dune?
x: Published in 1965, it is set on the desert planet Arrakis and is often cited as the best-selling science fiction novel.

q: Which author formulated the fictional Three Laws of Robotics?
x: The first law says a robot may not harm a human. Asimov explored the laws in stories collected in I, Robot.

q: In The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, what is the answer to life, the universe and everything?
x: The supercomputer Deep Thought takes 7.5 million years to compute it. Then it points out that nobody knew what the question was.

q: Who wrote A Wizard of Earthsea?
x: Published in 1968, it follows the young wizard Ged. Le Guin's book helped establish modern fantasy for young readers.

q: Who wrote the cyberpunk novel Neuromancer?
x: Published in 1984, it won the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards. It popularized the idea of cyberspace.

q: Which Philip K. Dick novel inspired the film Blade Runner?
a: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
The Man in the High Castle
x: The 1968 novel follows a bounty hunter chasing rogue androids. The 1982 film changed much of the plot.

q: Which H. G. Wells novel features the Eloi and the Morlocks?
a: The First Men in the Moon
x: Published in 1895, it describes two human descendants living in the year 802,701.

q: Which ancient Greek storyteller is traditionally credited with fables like The Tortoise and the Hare?
x: Aesop is said to have lived around 600 BC and possibly been a slave. Many fables credited to him were collected long after his time.

q: What were the first names of the Brothers Grimm?
x: They collected German folk tales and published them from 1812. They were also scholars of language and wrote a German dictionary.

q: Which French author published Cinderella and Puss in Boots in a 1697 collection?
x: His Tales of Mother Goose helped create the fairy-tale genre in literature. It included Sleeping Beauty and Little Red Riding Hood.

q: In which city is the famous statue of Hans Christian Andersen's Little Mermaid?
x: The bronze statue on the waterfront was unveiled in 1913. It is only about 1.25 meters tall.

q: Which sailor of One Thousand and One Nights goes on seven fantastic voyages?
x: Sinbad's tales feature giant birds and sea monsters. They were added to the collection by later translators and storytellers.

q: In Greek myth, who flew too close to the sun on wings made of wax and feathers?
x: His father Daedalus built the wings to escape Crete. Icarus ignored his warning and fell into the sea.

q: Which Greek hero beheaded the Gorgon Medusa?
x: Perseus used a polished shield as a mirror to avoid her stone-turning gaze. Pegasus sprang from her blood.

q: Which monster lived in the Labyrinth on Crete in Greek myth?
x: The Minotaur had a bull's head and a man's body. The hero Theseus killed it with help from Ariadne's thread.

q: What is the name of Thor's hammer in Norse mythology?
x: Mjolnir was made by dwarves. The Norse god of thunder used it against the giants.

q: Which Norse god is known as a shape-shifting trickster?
x: Loki fathered monsters such as the wolf Fenrir. In the myths he helps the gods at times and opposes them at others.

q: Which Roman poet wrote the Aeneid?
x: The epic tells of the Trojan hero Aeneas and the founding of Rome. Virgil died in 19 BC before finishing revisions.

q: Which Roman poet wrote the Metamorphoses?
x: Ovid's poem retells myths of transformation, from Daphne becoming a laurel tree to Narcissus becoming a flower.

q: In which ancient region was the Epic of Gilgamesh composed?
x: The poem was written on clay tablets in cuneiform. It is one of the oldest surviving works of literature.

q: Which ancient Indian epic tells the story of Rama and his wife Sita?
x: Traditionally credited to the sage Valmiki, it has been retold across South and Southeast Asia in many languages.

q: Which Chinese classic novel features the Monkey King, Sun Wukong?
x: The 16th-century novel follows a monk's pilgrimage to India to fetch sacred texts. It is one of China's Four Great Classical Novels.

q: Which German writer wrote the drama Faust?
x: Goethe worked on Faust for most of his adult life, finishing the second part in the year he died, 1832.

q: Pushkin's Eugene Onegin is unusual because it is a novel written in what form?
x: Pushkin called it a 'novel in verse' and wrote it in a special 14-line stanza now known as the Onegin stanza.

q: In which year did Ernest Hemingway win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
x: The Swedish Academy cited his mastery of narrative art, shown in The Old Man and the Sea. He was in Cuba and did not travel to Stockholm.

q: Who in 1907 became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
x: Kipling was 41 and remains the youngest-ever winner of the prize in literature.

q: Which Indian poet became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1913?
x: Tagore was honored for Gitanjali. He also wrote the lyrics of the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

q: Which author of Beloved won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature?
x: Morrison was the first African American woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. Beloved won the Pulitzer Prize in 1988.

q: What term describes the repetition of the same initial consonant sound, as in 'Peter Piper picked a peck'?
x: Alliteration is common in tongue twisters, poetry and advertising slogans. Old English poetry such as Beowulf relied on it.

q: What term describes a story whose characters and events symbolize deeper meanings, as in Animal Farm?
x: Pilgrim's Progress by John Bunyan is another famous allegory. Its characters have names like Christian and Mr. Worldly Wiseman.

q: How many lines does a limerick have?
x: Limericks follow an AABBA rhyme scheme and are usually humorous. Edward Lear popularized the form in the 1800s.

q: In Edward Lear's poem, what color is the boat in which the Owl and the Pussy-cat go to sea?
x: They sail with honey and plenty of money wrapped in a five-pound note, then marry on a hill where the bong-tree grows.

q: Which Lewis Carroll poem begins 'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves'?
x: It appears in Through the Looking-Glass. Carroll's invented words, like chortle and galumphing, have entered English.

q: Which T. S. Eliot poetry collection inspired the musical Cats?
a: Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
x: Eliot published it in 1939 and signed it with his nickname, Old Possum. Andrew Lloyd Webber set it to music in 1981.

q: Which 1922 poem by T. S. Eliot begins 'April is the cruellest month'?
a: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
x: Ezra Pound heavily edited the draft, cutting it down to a landmark of modernist poetry.

q: Which Oscar Wilde play features the formidable Lady Bracknell?
x: The 1895 comedy is subtitled 'A Trivial Comedy for Serious People.' Lady Bracknell famously exclaims 'A handbag?'

q: Which George Bernard Shaw play inspired the musical My Fair Lady?
x: Shaw's 1913 play follows a phonetics professor teaching a flower seller to speak like a lady. Its title comes from a Greek myth.

q: Which Russian playwright wrote The Seagull and Uncle Vanya?
x: Chekhov was also a medical doctor. His plays, including Three Sisters, are staples of world theater.

q: Which Norwegian dramatist wrote A Doll's House?
x: Premiered in 1879, the play caused controversy when its heroine Nora walked out on her family in the final scene.

q: Which Arthur Miller play is set during the Salem witch trials?
x: Written in 1953, it used the 1692 trials as an allegory for McCarthyism in the United States.

q: Which Tennessee Williams play features the character Blanche DuBois?
a: Cat on a Hot Tin Roof
x: The 1947 play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama. Marlon Brando starred in the 1951 film adaptation.

q: Which Irish writer wrote the play Waiting for Godot?
x: Beckett first wrote it in French in the early 1950s. It features two men waiting for someone who never arrives.

q: Which Dickens novel opens with 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?
x: The 1859 novel is set in London and Paris before and during the French Revolution.

q: Which novel opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael.'?
x: Melville's 1851 whaling novel sold poorly during his lifetime. Its opening is among the most famous in American literature.

q: Which novel begins 'Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way'?
x: Tolstoy's 1878 novel opens with this line. It follows a married woman whose affair challenges Russian high society.

q: Which Beat Generation author wrote On the Road?
x: Published in 1957, it was reportedly typed on a single long scroll of paper in just a few weeks.

q: Which author wrote the World War II satire Catch-22?
x: Published in 1961, the novel gave English the phrase 'catch-22' for a no-win situation with contradictory rules.

q: Which horror writer wrote The Shining?
x: King's 1977 novel is set in the isolated Overlook Hotel. Stanley Kubrick adapted it into a 1980 film.

q: Which French author wrote The Stranger?
x: Published in 1942, the novel opens with the narrator Meursault learning of his mother's death. Camus won the Nobel Prize in 1957.

q: Which author wrote the 1981 novel Midnight's Children?
x: It won the Booker Prize in 1981 and again earned the Booker of Bookers award in 1993. Its narrator was born at the moment of India's independence.

q: In which city did Franz Kafka live most of his life?
x: Kafka was born in Prague in 1883 and wrote in German. Most of his major works were published after his death.

q: Which Hemingway novel, set in the Spanish Civil War, takes its title from a John Donne meditation?
x: Donne's lines include 'never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.' Hemingway published the novel in 1940.

q: What is the title of Lewis Carroll's 1871 sequel to Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
x: The sequel's world is based on a chess game. Carroll's original draft of the first book was titled Alice's Adventures Under Ground.

q: What are the workers in Willy Wonka's chocolate factory called?
x: In Dahl's first version of the book, the factory workers were African pygmies. He revised them into the orange-skinned Oompa-Loompas in later editions.

q: What is the name of Bilbo Baggins's sword in The Hobbit?
x: The elvish blade glows blue when orcs or goblins are near. Bilbo later gives it to his nephew Frodo.

q: What is the name of Mr. Darcy's estate in Pride and Prejudice?
x: Elizabeth Bennet's visit to Pemberley changes her opinion of Darcy. Netherfield is the house rented by Mr. Bingley.

q: In Little Women, which March sister dreams of being a writer?
x: Jo is based on Louisa May Alcott herself. Her real name is Josephine.

q: What is the name of Phileas Fogg's French valet in Around the World in Eighty Days?
x: Passepartout means 'goes everywhere' in French. He is Fogg's loyal companion on the whole wager.

q: In The Count of Monte Cristo, in which prison is Edmond Dantes held?
x: The Chateau d'If is a real island fortress off Marseille. Dumas's story made it a world-famous tourist site.

q: What is Sherlock Holmes's fictional London address?
x: When the stories were written, no 221 existed on Baker Street. A museum now stands at the address.

q: What nationality is Agatha Christie's detective Hercule Poirot?
x: Poirot is a retired Belgian police officer living in England. He debuted in 1920 in The Mysterious Affair at Styles.

q: In Orwell's 1984, who is the leader whose face appears on posters saying 'is watching you'?
x: Big Brother is the figurehead of the Party. The slogan on the posters says 'Big Brother is watching you.'

q: Which poet wrote 'Ozymandias'?
x: Shelley wrote it in 1817 about a ruined statue of a once-great king in the desert. The poem reflects on the fading of power.

q: Which poet wrote 'The Charge of the Light Brigade'?
x: Tennyson wrote it in 1854 shortly after reading a newspaper report of the doomed cavalry attack in the Crimean War.

q: Who is the teenage narrator of The Catcher in the Rye?
x: Holden recounts a few days in New York after being expelled from his prep school, Pencey.

q: In The Hobbit, who loses the magic ring to Bilbo after a game of riddles in the dark?
x: Gollum bets the ring against Bilbo in the riddle game. Bilbo wins by asking 'What have I got in my pocket?'

q: Which Charles Dickens story features the miser Ebenezer Scrooge?
x: Three ghosts visit Scrooge on Christmas Eve and change his heart.
